claims.text: Premelting onset in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles is governed by the interplay between high configurational entropy and lattice strain from atomic-size mismatch.
Atomic-size mismatch produces local lattice strain in these nanoparticles.
Limited atomic mobility kinetically freezes heterogeneous regions with high defect concentrations.
Defects concentrated at surfaces and grain boundaries act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for liquid-like domains.
The initial particles are equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles a few nanometers in diameter.
The initial particles are single-phase, homogenized solid solutions.
The particles will be heated from room temperature through approximately 800–1600 K at a few kelvin per minute under argon or high vacuum.
Defects and interfaces generated by lattice distortion form heterogeneous regions with reduced cohesive energy.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the overall HEA solid solution.
Regions of high lattice strain have locally weakened bonding that promotes early localized disordering.
Localized strained or defective regions partially liquefy before the bulk of a nanoparticle melts.
Localized premelting produces a broader melting transition than occurs in simpler, less-strained nanoparticle systems.
Relative to size- and processing-matched bimetallic controls, the HEA nanoparticles will melt more gradually and heterogeneously.
Surface- or defect-associated liquid-like regions will appear below the temperature of complete melting.
Bimetallic nanoparticles typically show sharper, more spatially uniform melting without pronounced defect-site premelting.
The proposed mechanism is limited to nanoscale, equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEA particles in which kinetic limitations restrict atomic mobility.
Composition, particle size, and synthesis route can change defect density or lattice distortion and therefore alter the mechanism's applicability.
Premelting offsets and strain-dependent melting kinetics may vary with particle-size distribution and synthesis-induced microstructure.
